Kaza and Kraft drew the excerpt from Cleary's *Entry into the Inconceivable: An Introduction to Hua-yen Buddhism* (University of Hawai‘i Press, 1983), 66–68; that earlier container will receive its own source house if the essay cites material beyond this excerpt. The underlying Chinese passage belongs to the *Huayan wujiao zhiguan* (華嚴五教止觀, *Calming and Contemplation in the Five Teachings of Huayan*), conventionally attributed to Dushun (557–640), at Taishō canon T45, no. 1867, 513a28–513b21. Modern scholarship disputes that attribution, so the record preserves it as conventional provenance rather than settled authorship. ## Chicago 18 forms **Full note:** Dushun (attributed), “The Jewel Net of Indra,” trans. Thomas Cleary, in *Dharma Rain: Sources of Buddhist Environmentalism*, ed. Stephanie Kaza and Kenneth Kraft (Boston: Shambhala, 2000), 58–60. **Shortened note:** Dushun, “Jewel Net of Indra,” 58–60. **Bibliography:** Dushun (attributed). “The Jewel Net of Indra.” Translated by Thomas Cleary. In *Dharma Rain: Sources of Buddhist Environmentalism*, edited by Stephanie Kaza and Kenneth Kraft, 58–60. Boston: Shambhala, 2000. ## Essay use ### Source's relevant contribution The passage makes each jewel of Indra's net a site in which the remaining jewels appear, then follows the reflections recursively so that the whole net is implicated within every local jewel. This is the primary-text pathway for the essay's image of a field whose members disclose one another through their relations. ### Licensed essay use - Establish the jewel-net as a Huayan image of reciprocal reflection and recursive implication. - Give the myth history a textual route from the Indian figure of Indra into Chinese Huayan philosophical elaboration. - Place the image beside Hephaestus's bonds as the source-bearing half of the essay's Offered double-net reading. ### Claim boundary This passage does not derive apoha, Nāgārjuna's account of dependent arising, Kashmir Śaiva *saṃkalpa*, QL's `0/1`, or a theory of digital networks and commons governance. Those relations must be argued across their own sources. The Dushun attribution remains conventional and contested, and Cleary's printed pages must be collated before any English wording is promoted as quotation-ready. ## Passages and excerpts ### Material metadata - **Selected translation:** Dushun (attributed), “The Jewel Net of Indra,” trans. The journal-level metadata (author, title, volume, year, page span) is verified; a PDF of the German original has been located on the journal's own site (rhm.uni-koeln.de) but its sentences have not yet been extracted into this house. An English translation exists as "The Song of Ares and Aphrodite: On the Relationship between the Odyssey and the Iliad," in G. M. Wright and P. V. Jones, eds., *Homer: German Scholarship in Translation* (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1997), reported at pages 249–262; that page span is unverified and the translation volume has not been added as a container of its own. Until extraction, the German article is the citable object and the English span is provisional. ## Chicago 18 forms **Full note:** Walter Burkert, "Das Lied von Ares und Aphrodite: Zum Verhältnis von Odyssee und Ilias," *Rheinisches Museum für Philologie* 103 (1960): 130–44. **Shortened note:** Burkert, "Lied von Ares und Aphrodite," 130–44. **Bibliography:** Burkert, Walter. "Das Lied von Ares und Aphrodite: Zum Verhältnis von Odyssee und Ilias." *Rheinisches Museum für Philologie* 103 (1960): 130–44. *English-translation forms (page span to verify before use):* Walter Burkert, "The Song of Ares and Aphrodite: On the Relationship between the Odyssey and the Iliad," in *Homer: German Scholarship in Translation*, ed. G. M. Wright and P. V. Jones (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1997), 249–62. ## Source scholarship Burkert's 1960 article is a classic of Homeric philology on precisely the passage the essay reads. Its demonstrandum is intertextual: through repeated lines, formulas, and phrases shared between the Demodocus song and the divine comedy of *Iliad* 1, Burkert argues that the song presupposes the *Iliad* — the Odyssey-poet is not drawing on a common stock but composing against a known text, and the gods' comic detachment in Odyssey 8 is intelligible as a deliberate transformation of the Iliadic divine apparatus. The article thereby became a standard reference in the analyst/unitarian and neoanalysis debates about the relation of the two epics, and any use of the song's poetics that ignores it is scholarly incomplete. What makes the article close to load-bearing for the essay is the reading reported at its interpretive center: the song as a celebration of *technē* over *physis*. On this account — reported via the Bryn Mawr Classical Review notice (BMCR 1998.11.09) of the Wright and Jones translation volume — the craft-god's victory over the war-god is the Odyssey-poet's programmatic answer to Iliadic force: the poem that begins from cunning and homecoming stages, inside its own performance scene, the defeat of the strongest god by the cleverest. A 1960 philological classic thus already reads the episode as a verdict about craft-intelligence versus violent strength, which is exactly the hinge on which the essay turns the scene toward its own technological reading. The essay does not need Burkert to go further than this — and he does not: his frame is poetics and intertextuality, not technology. The evidentiary situation must be kept honest. No sentence of Burkert's — German or English — has yet been extracted and verified by this house. The technē-over-physis characterisation currently rests on a reviewer's summary of a translation of the article. That is a legitimate pointer for locating the argument but not a quotable authority; the German PDF is in hand as a locator, and extraction of the exact sentences (with page numbers in RhM 103) is the single task standing between this house and citation-grade use. ## Essay use ### Source's relevant contribution Burkert supplies the philological control: a canonical scholarly demonstration that the Demodocus song is a deliberate, intertextually knowing composition whose point is the victory of craft over force — securing the essay against the objection that its craft-versus-strength reading is a modern imposition on a light entertainment. ### Licensed essay use - Cite the article as the standard demonstration that the song presupposes *Iliad* 1 and transforms its divine comedy. - Once sentences are extracted: attribute the technē-over-physis reading of the song to Burkert, with exact wording and page. - Serve the myth history as the philological anchor of the episode's scholarly reception. ### Claim boundary Burkert's claim concerns Odyssey/Iliad intertextuality and the song's poetics — craft over force as a poetic program. He does not read the net as proto-technology-critique, does not treat surveillance, apparatus, or enframing, and says nothing about modernity. The passage from his technē/physis verdict to the essay's enframing reading is the essay's own Argued move. Until the German text is extracted, even the technē-over-physis attribution must be flagged in draft prose as reported via BMCR. ## Passages and excerpts ### Material metadata - **Original:** *Rheinisches Museum für Philologie* 103 (1960): 130–144; PDF located at rhm.uni-koeln.de, not yet extracted. - **English translation:** Wright and Jones, *Homer: German Scholarship in Translation* (Oxford, 1997), reported pp. 249–262 (unverified). - **Access provenance:** journal metadata verified; interpretive content currently known through BMCR 1998.11.09 (review of Wright and Jones) and the article's standing in the secondary literature. No direct wording held. ## Passage card — `burkert-1960-lied-ares-aphrodite-q001` — technē over physis **Reported thesis (not yet quotable):** The Demodocus song celebrates *technē* over *physis*: the craft-god's victory over the war-god is the Odyssey-poet's programmatic answer to Iliadic force, composed in demonstrable awareness of *Iliad* 1. - **Locator:** RhM 103 (1960): 130–44 (article-level; sentence-level locator pending extraction); English trans. reported at Wright and Jones 1997, 249–62. - **Status:** acquisition-required; reported via BMCR 1998.11.09 review of the English translation volume. - **Verification:** Coordinator, 2026-07-18; article identity and page span verified against journal records; thesis wording taken from the BMCR reviewer's characterisation, not from Burkert's text; German PDF located but sentences not extracted. Verify the English translation's page span (reported 249–262) against the Wright and Jones volume; correct the provisional Chicago form. 3. Brown — Ares, Aphrodite, and the Laughter of the Gods (1989) ## Bibliographic identity The target work is Christopher G. Brown, "Ares, Aphrodite, and the Laughter of the Gods," *Phoenix* 43, no. 4 (1989): 283–293. Journal metadata (author, title, volume, issue, year, page span) is verified against the journal's records. The article itself sits behind the JSTOR paywall and has not been acquired; the two verified quotations below were collated from Brown's own later public presentation of the same argument for the Kosmos Society (Center for Hellenic Studies community), where he restates the article's thesis in his own words. That channel verifies wording and authorship of the claims but not their page-locations within *Phoenix* 43, which await collation against the article. ## Chicago 18 forms **Full note:** Christopher G. Brown, "Ares, Aphrodite, and the Laughter of the Gods," *Phoenix* 43, no. 4 (1989): 283–93. **Shortened note:** Brown, "Laughter of the Gods," 283–93. **Bibliography:** Brown, Christopher G. "Ares, Aphrodite, and the Laughter of the Gods." *Phoenix* 43, no. 4 (1989): 283–93. *Page-level locators within 283–93 cannot yet be supplied in notes; until collation, notes must cite the full article span.* ## Source scholarship Brown reads Hephaestus's treatment of the trapped lovers against Greek social practice rather than as free-floating divine comedy. His thesis, in his own later formulation: "Hephaestus' treatment of the lovers reflects the use of mockery and abuse in dealing with adultery, and… this has something to say about the dynamics of shame in early Greek culture." The gods' unquenchable laughter (ἄσβεστος γέλως, 8.326) is not incidental amusement but the operative punishment: in a shame-culture, ridicule before one's peers is the sanction, and Hephaestus's summons to the gods — his insistence that they come and see (ἴδησθε, 8.306–7) — is the deliberate production of that sanction's audience. The argument's second movement grounds this in attested practice: "In many Greek communities various devices were used to expose criminals and adulterers to public shaming and ridicule. In this light, the story of Olympian adultery has been shaped by social reality." Brown assembles the comparative evidence for institutionalised exposure — the parading, display, and ritualised mockery of adulterers known from various Greek communities — and argues that the Olympian scene is modelled on it. The scene's machinery of capture, display, and communal laughter is therefore not a poet's whimsy but a transposition of a real social apparatus for producing shame onto the divine plane, which is also why its comedy lands: the original audience recognised the institution. For the essay this is the indispensable bridge. Brown establishes, on ordinary philological and social-historical grounds, that the scene is *about* exposure and public shaming as a social apparatus — that display before witnesses is the point of the trap, not a by-product. This is the scholarly control that lets the essay's surveillance/spectacle reading proceed without anachronism: the essay does not have to smuggle "staged public evidence" into the text, because the classical scholarship already finds an exposure-apparatus there. What the essay adds — the reading of that apparatus as the mythic body of technological enframing — begins where Brown stops. ## Essay use ### Source's relevant contribution Brown supplies the shame-culture control: the scholarly demonstration that capture-plus-display-plus-communal-laughter in Od. 8 transposes a real Greek social apparatus of exposure and ridicule, making the scene's spectacle structural rather than incidental. ### Licensed essay use - Establish that Hephaestus's staging of the lovers reflects attested Greek practices of mockery and public exposure of adulterers (q001, q002). - License the reading of ἴδησθε (8.306–7) and ἄσβεστος γέλως (8.326) as apparatus: evidence-display and sanction-by-spectacle within a shame-culture. - Serve the myth history's account of the episode's social-historical reception. ### Claim boundary Brown's claims concern shame-culture and comic poetics: the scene as shaped by social practices of exposure and ridicule. He makes no claim about surveillance technology, enframing, spectacle in the Debordian sense, or any modern extension; the technological reading remains the essay's own Argued development. [Publication venue and year unresolved; PDF accessible at austriaca.at, Austrian Academy of Sciences.] ## Source scholarship Phillips reads the Demodocus song as the ideal aetiology of Greek adultery law: the earliest and fullest narrative display of the legal pattern that the historical poleis institutionalised. On his reading, Hephaestus does not act as a jealous cuckold improvising revenge; he exercises "rights as husband and householder to apprehend and detain Ares" — the self-help seizure of the *moichos* taken in the act, a practice attested across the Greek world and, on the evidence of this very passage, already recognisable by around 700 BCE. The trap, the detention in the bonds, the summoning of witnesses, and the refusal to release until satisfaction: each element corresponds to a step in the legally sanctioned treatment of the adulterer caught *ep' autophōrōi*. Two philological details carry the argument's precision. First, the hapax μοιχάγρια (Od. 8.332) — formed like ζωάγρια, the price paid for a life spared — names the adulterer's fine: the compensation the captured *moichos* pays for his release. The word exists in Greek exactly once, and it exists as a legal-financial term embedded in this scene; the scene thus contains its own juridical vocabulary. Second, Phillips reads the Poseidon exchange (8.344–58) as formal surety-law (ἐγγύη) in complete procedural sequence: charge stated, penalty demanded, restitution framed against the ἕεδνα (the bride-price Hephaestus paid, 8.318, now the measure of what relation-as-account owes him back), a third party standing surety for payment, and release upon the surety's pledge. Hephaestus's initial refusal — wretched are the pledges of the wretched — and Poseidon's personal guarantee that he will pay if Ares defaults are the recognisable form of the institution, not a courtly ornament. For the essay this carries two loads, and it is worth stating them exactly. (a) The apparatus's juridical completeness — detection, detention, tribunal of witnesses, fine — is not the essay's projection onto the scene but the scene's own legal anatomy, established by a legal historian on independent grounds (pp. 8–9 of the accessible PDF). (b) The surety exchange is REAL legal form: when the essay argues its trust-closure — the apparatus cannot conclude; only a person standing surety concludes it; Poseidon's ἐγγύη, not the net, releases the bond — that argument rests on an institution Greek law recognises, not on a metaphor. The Lloyd translation was reissued in paperback by the University of Chicago Press in 1991; the two printings are believed to share pagination, but this has not been confirmed, and the consulted edition must be pinned when a physical or fully readable copy is acquired. All page references in this house (pp. 3, 13, 272–73, and the ch. 10 span 269–75) currently follow the 1978 Harvester printing as cited in the verifying secondary literature. ## Chicago 18 forms **Full note:** Marcel Detienne and Jean-Pierre Vernant, *Cunning Intelligence in Greek Culture and Society*, trans. Janet Lloyd (Hassocks: Harvester Press, 1978), 3. **Shortened note:** Detienne and Vernant, *Cunning Intelligence*, 3. **Bibliography:** Detienne, Marcel, and Jean-Pierre Vernant. *Cunning Intelligence in Greek Culture and Society*. Translated by Janet Lloyd. Hassocks: Harvester Press, 1978. First published as *Les ruses de l'intelligence: La métis des Grecs*. Paris: Flammarion, 1974. *If the 1991 Chicago paperback is pinned as the consulted edition, the imprint in all three forms changes to (Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1991) with a first-published note; pagination must then be re-collated.* ## Source scholarship Detienne and Vernant reconstruct *mētis* — cunning, resourceful, polymorphic intelligence — as a coherent category of Greek thought that the Greeks themselves never theorised in a treatise, and that philosophy after Plato actively occluded. Their method is to read the category out of its scattered operations: hunting and trapping, fishing, weaving and net-making, navigation and the pilot's art, medicine, rhetoric, the charioteer's turn, and the craftsman's work. What emerges is not a loose family resemblance but, in their words, a "complex but very coherent body of mental attitudes and intellectual behavior" (p. 3): an intelligence that operates in shifting, ambiguous situations, that binds itself to the fluid and polymorphic in order to master it, and whose instruments — the trap, the net, the woven circle, the bond — reproduce its own suppleness in material form. The book's structural logic is exactly the logic of the Odyssey 8 gnome (lame Hephaestus catches the swiftest of the gods, 8.329–32). The signature of *mētis*, Detienne and Vernant argue, is to "revers[e] the 'natural' outcome of the encounter," because "whatever the strength of god or man, there always comes a time when he confronts one stronger than himself" (p. 13): force meets its ceiling; cunning has none, since it wins precisely where it is weaker. Hephaestus is one of their canonical carriers of this reversal. His crooked feet are "the visible symbol" of "his metis, his wise thoughts and his craftsman's intelligence" (p. 272) — the deformity is not the negation of his power but its emblem, a "double and divergent orientation" that lets him "dominate shifting, fluid powers" (p. 273), the walking-both-ways of an intelligence at home in ambiguity. Chapter 10, "The Circle and the Bond," is the chapter most directly on-point for the essay and the one passage-block still awaiting extraction. There the circle, the net, and the *desmos* are treated as the canonical instruments of *mētis*: the bond is the woven circle that closes around a polymorphic victim, defeating shape-shifting by enclosing every shape at once — the victim cannot out-turn what has no open direction. This is the precise scholarly frame for Hephaestus's δεσμοὶ τεχνήεντες: bonds finer than spider-silk, invisible even to the gods, encircling the bed itself. The chapter's exact sentences on the Ares–Aphrodite bonds have been located to the chapter span (pp. 269–75) but not yet transcribed; the accessible scan is not machine-readable, and quotation waits on the print edition. The book's authority for the essay is that of a foundational structuralist study: it established *mētis* as a live scholarly category, and subsequent classical scholarship on trickery, craft, and binding routinely routes through it. The three verified quotations above were collated not from the book directly but from a scholarly article quoting the 1978 Lloyd translation — Jay Dolmage, "'Breathe Upon Us an Even Flame': Hephaestus, History, and the Body of Rhetoric," *Rhetoric Review* 25, no. 2 (2006) — which is a lawful but second-hand verification channel; the wording is treated as reliable, the print collation as still owed. ## Essay use ### Source's relevant contribution Detienne and Vernant supply the scholarly control establishing that the bond, the net, and the reversal of strength by craft are not incidental furniture of the Demodocus song but instruments and logic of a coherent Greek category of intelligence — and that Hephaestus is that category's divine craftsman-bearer. ### Licensed essay use - Establish *mētis* as a coherent Greek craft-intelligence category with the bond and net among its canonical instruments (q001, q004). - Ground the essay's reading of the lame-catches-swift gnome (Od. 8.329–32) in the reversal-logic of *mētis* (q002). - Ground the reading of Hephaestus's lameness as the emblem of his craft-intelligence rather than a mere defect (q003). - Serve the myth history and the ancient-philosophy history as the standard scholarly reconstruction of the category. ### Claim boundary Detienne and Vernant establish *mētis* and the bond as a Greek craft-intelligence category; they do not connect the Ares–Aphrodite episode to modern technology, surveillance, enframing, or Heidegger. Every step from their category to the essay's technological reading — σκοπιή as surveillance, the *desmos* as capture-apparatus, the staged ἴδησθε as evidence-production — is the essay's own Argued or Offered development and may not be attributed to this source. ## Passages and excerpts ### Material metadata - **Selected edition (provisional):** Lloyd translation, Harvester Press, 1978; The New York Public Library catalogue confirms translator, publisher, year, pagination, and its status as a translation of *Ursprung und Gegenwart*; Open Library corroborates ISBN 0821402196 and OCLC 9323637. ## Chicago 18 forms **Full note:** Jean Gebser, *The Ever-Present Origin*, trans. Translated by Noel Barstad and Algis Mickunas. Ohio University Press, 1985. ## Essay use ### Source's relevant contribution Gebser presents consciousness structures through their representative visual, linguistic, and intellectual forms. The mental-rational structure receives its historical expression in the Renaissance discovery and construction of perspective: Giotto's tentative externalisation of depth, Petrarch's discovery of landscape, Alberti's visual pyramid, and Leonardo's perfected optical and technical articulation. Perspective thereby makes space and ego-consciousness visible while fixing the observer and observed within a sector. Aperspectivity names liberation from that structure's exclusive validity through the co-presence and transparency of the structures, not their amalgamation. For the zero–subject historical braid, this is a stadial account: integral consciousness is a higher mutation that makes the mental-rational structure's constituting conditions available without abolishing its powers. The braid's `180°→360°` QL articulation is authorial; Gebser supplies the historical problem and the aperspectival/integral direction. His own presentation gives the Return of Zero a methodological precedent of unusual exactness: a historical mutation is read from changes in the means by which a world is rendered—painting, optics, language, thought, science. The essay extends this procedure into the Internet/AI field, where prompt, memory, retrieval, permissions, policy, provenance, feedback, and relation have become operational conditions of intelligence. That contextual mutation and its `0/1` formalisation are the essay's argument from Gebser's method, not claims attributed to Gebser. ### Passage map | Locator | Source operation | Essay consumer | Relation | |---|---|---|---| | pp. 1–3 | Mutations are read through visible, tangible, audible, linguistic, artistic, and scientific manifestations;
